The Red-fronted parakeet (Cyanoramphus novaezelandiae) is a medium-sized psittacine endemic to New Zealand, where it occupies a range of forested and scrubland habitats. Field studies examining the early developmental stages of this species have documented that freshly laid eggs weigh approximately 6.25 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.25 grams], a value that reflects the considerable maternal investment in yolk and albumen prior to the onset of incubation. The incubation period itself is strongly temperature-dependent, and under controlled conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days]. This developmental duration is typical for parrots of this body size and aligns with reports for other Cyanoramphus taxa. Upon emergence, the altricial nestlings exhibit a wet weight at birth of about 5.5 grams [Wwb = about 5.5 grams], which is notably low relative to the ultimate adult masses achieved later in life. This modest neonatal mass underscores the highly altricial state of the hatchlings, which are entirely dependent on parental brooding and provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition during the initial weeks post-hatching.

As the nestlings progress through the brooding phase and into the fledgling stage, their growth trajectory accelerates markedly under the thermal conditions typical of an actively brooded nest, which hovers near 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The relatively rapid onset of puberty in this species, compared to larger Psittaciformes, likely reflects an adaptive life-history strategy favoring early breeding in unpredictable island environments where adult mortality can be high due to introduced predators.

Reproductive output in the Red-fronted parakeet is characterized by a relatively modest maximum reproductive rate. Under optimal thermal conditions (maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), females produce approximately 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2 eggs per clutch] and raise approximately 3.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 3.5 clutches per year], yielding an annual output of about 7 eggs. The age at first successful reproduction is deferred until approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching] when measured at a body temperat at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]ure of 41.3 °C. This delay between the attainment of sexual maturity and the onset of actual breeding is a common pattern among parrots and is interpreted as a period during which young birds acquire critical foraging skills and establish breeding territories.

Considerable sexual size dimorphism is evident in the ultimate wet weight attained by adult Red-fronted parakeets, a trait that reflects differential reproductive investment between the sexes. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of approximately 81.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 81.5 grams], while males, which are generally the larger sex in this species, attain an ultimate wet weight of about 88 grams [Wwi = about 88 grams]. This divergence in mass is not merely a product of skeletal size differences but is also linked to the energetic demands of egg production in females versus the physical competition and territory defense undertaken by males. Such dimorphism is consistent with patterns observed in other members of the genus Cyanoramphus, although the magnitude of the difference in Red-fronted parakeets is somewhat less pronounced than in some of its more sexually segregated congeners.

Longevity data for Cyanoramphus novaezelandiae, derived both from long-term field mark-recapture studies and from captive colony records, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4,526 days [am = approximately 4,526 days] when individuals are measured at a stable body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which equates to roughly 12.4 years. This lifespan is comparatively long for a bird of this body mass and is typical of the slow life-history pace characterizing many island-endemic psittacines, which have evolved in environments with low extrinsic mortality. The life-history strategy of this species, featuring delayed first reproduction and extended lifespan, prioritizes adult survival and repeated breeding attempts over a single reproductive bout. This strategy, however, makes the species particularly vulnerable to sudden increases in adult mortality from introduced mammalian predators.
